meta: An AI team splits roles just like a newsroom. The orchestrator (lead agent) takes the job, breaks it down and writes clear instructions for each subagent: what to find, where, and in what format.

muc.title: Like a newsroom
muc.text: A newsroom has an editor-in-chief, reporters and proofreaders. Multi-agent splits roles the same way.

muc.title: Give clear assignments
muc.text: The orchestrator takes the job from you, breaks it down, and writes clear instructions for each subagent: what to find, where, and in what format. Vague instructions mean subagents end up doing the same work twice.

muc.title: Each worker has its own toolkit
muc.text: The subagents are specialists. Each has exactly the tools it needs: one searches the web, one reads spreadsheets, one writes.

muc.title: Another pair of eyes
muc.text: Add a critic agent, called a reviewer: it writes nothing, it just looks for mistakes, checks sources and points out gaps. Two different pairs of eyes catch errors one would miss.

muc.title: One result for you
muc.text: Finally, the orchestrator puts everything together into one result for you.

muc.title: MCP and A2A
muc.text: Agents talking to each other need shared standards too. MCP lets agents plug into tools. And A2A, short for Agent to Agent, is the standard for one company's agent to hand work to another company's agent.

muc.title: Your own team of two
muc.text: Open two chat windows. Window one writes the article. Window two plays a tough critic. Pass the article back and forth twice, and you'll see the later version is much better.

muc.title: Teams get messy too
muc.text: But every team gets messy sometimes. The last part: when multi-agent goes wrong.
